topic.en: Three texts: the clocks inside plants, how the lithium-ion battery changed technology, and the argument about antibiotics on farms.
topic.kk: Үш мәтін: өсімдіктердің ішкі сағаты, литий-ионды аккумулятор техниканы қалай өзгертті және мал шаруашылығындағы антибиотиктер туралы талқы.
topic.ru: Три текста: внутренние часы растений, как литий-ионный аккумулятор изменил технику, и спор об антибиотиках в животноводстве.

paragraphs.text: Long before scientists had any idea how it worked, gardeners knew that many plants behave as if they could tell the time. Some flowers open in the morning and close in the evening; the leaves of beans and many other plants rise during the day and fold down at night. In the eighteenth century a French astronomer placed a plant in a dark cupboard and found that its leaves continued to open and close on roughly the usual schedule, even though the plant could not see the sun. The rhythm, it seemed, came from inside the plant rather than from the light. Similar movements had been described by ancient writers, who assumed that the plants were simply following the sun.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: That observation is now regarded as the first experimental evidence of what biologists call a circadian clock, an internal timer that runs on a cycle of about twenty-four hours. Such clocks have since been found in almost every kind of living thing, from bacteria to humans. In plants, the clock is not located in a single organ, as it is in the brains of animals; every cell contains its own copy, built from a set of genes whose products switch one another on and off in a loop that takes roughly a day to complete. The genes involved differ between plants and animals, which suggests that clocks evolved independently more than once.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: Left entirely alone, the clock drifts, because its natural period is rarely exactly twenty-four hours. It is kept in time by signals from the environment, above all by light at dawn and dusk and by the daily rise and fall of temperature. Plants detect light through several families of light-sensitive proteins, some of which respond to red light and others to blue. Each morning these signals reset the clock slightly, in the same way that a person might adjust a watch that runs a few minutes fast. Temperature signals are especially important for plants growing in shade or under snow, where light gives little information.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: The clock controls a surprising proportion of what a plant does. Studies of the thale cress, a small weed that has become the standard laboratory plant, have found that the activity of around a third of its genes rises and falls over the day. The plant prepares for photosynthesis before dawn, so that it is ready to use light as soon as it arrives, and it produces chemicals that deter insects at the times of day when those insects are most active. It also rations the starch it has stored during the day so that the supply lasts almost exactly until the next sunrise. Some flowers time the release of their scent to match the hours when their pollinators are active.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: The clock also measures the seasons. Many plants flower only when days reach a particular length, and they judge this by comparing the timing of light with the phase of their internal clock. A plant that needs long days to flower will do so only if light is still present at a point in the evening when the clock expects darkness. This mechanism explains why some crops flower at the wrong time when they are moved far to the north or south of the region where they were originally grown. Plants that flower in autumn use the same mechanism in reverse, flowering only when nights become long enough.
paragraphs.label: E

paragraphs.text: A clock that matches the environment appears to give a plant a real advantage. In one experiment, researchers grew plants whose internal clocks ran on cycles of twenty or twenty-eight hours under artificial days of matching or mismatched length. Plants whose clocks matched their day grew larger, fixed more carbon and survived better than those that did not. The result suggests that the clock is not merely a curiosity but an important factor in how efficiently a plant uses its resources. Similar advantages have been reported in studies of bacteria whose clocks were matched or mismatched with their environment.
paragraphs.label: F

paragraphs.text: These findings have attracted the interest of plant breeders. Several of the genes involved in crop domestication turn out to be clock genes, altered in ways that allowed crops such as barley and soybean to be grown at new latitudes. Breeders are now examining whether adjusting the clock could produce varieties better suited to changing climates, for example by shifting flowering to avoid periods of heat or drought. Some researchers have also suggested that the timing of spraying and harvesting could be matched to the daily rhythms of crops. Such adjustments could be made using conventional breeding as well as newer genetic methods.
paragraphs.label: G

paragraphs.text: The study of plant clocks has also changed ideas about timing in medicine. The discovery that many processes in the body follow daily cycles has led researchers to ask whether some treatments work better at particular times of day, a question that plant biologists had been asking about their own subjects for decades. The humble bean leaf, folding itself up in a dark cupboard nearly three centuries ago, turned out to be the first clue to one of the most widespread features of life on Earth. Plant clocks, in other words, are not a botanical curiosity but part of a pattern shared across nearly all living things.
paragraphs.label: H

paragraphs.text: Few technologies have shaped daily life in the past thirty years as thoroughly as the rechargeable lithium-ion battery. It powers phones, laptops and cameras, has made electric cars practical, and is increasingly used to store electricity from wind and solar farms. Yet the battery that seems so ordinary today took decades to develop, passed through several dangerous dead ends and still depends on materials whose supply raises difficult questions. Its history illustrates how long it can take for a laboratory discovery to become an everyday object, and few people who use one think about the chemistry inside.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: The attraction of lithium is easy to explain. It is the lightest metal and gives up its outer electron very readily, which means that a battery based on it can store a large amount of energy for its weight. The difficulty is that pure lithium metal is highly reactive. Early rechargeable batteries that used it in the 1970s and 1980s tended to grow thin, needle-like deposits of metal on one electrode each time they were charged, and these could eventually pierce the separator between the electrodes, causing a short circuit and sometimes a fire. Several manufacturers withdrew such batteries after fires were reported, and research on lithium metal slowed for many years.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: The solution was to avoid using lithium metal at all. In the modern battery, lithium is present only as ions, atoms that have lost an electron, which move back and forth between two electrodes made of other materials. The positive electrode is usually a metal oxide with a layered structure, and the negative electrode is normally made of graphite, a form of carbon whose sheets of atoms can hold lithium ions between them. Because the ions are stored in these structures rather than deposited as metal, the battery is far safer. Graphite was not the first choice; earlier designs used other forms of carbon that stored less lithium.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: Charging and discharging follow a simple cycle. When the battery is charged, an external supply pushes lithium ions out of the positive electrode, through a liquid called the electrolyte and across a porous separator, into the graphite, while electrons travel the same way through the external circuit. When the battery is used, the process reverses: the ions return to the positive electrode through the electrolyte, and the electrons, forced to take the long way round through the device, provide the current that powers it. The rate at which ions can move through the electrolyte limits how quickly a battery can be charged, which is why fast charging generates heat.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: The first commercial lithium-ion batteries went on sale in the early 1990s, and three of the scientists who developed the key materials were later awarded a Nobel Prize. Since then the energy that can be stored in a battery of a given weight has roughly tripled, while the price has fallen by around ninety per cent. These improvements came less from any single breakthrough than from thousands of small changes to the materials, the manufacturing process and the electronics that control charging. Much of this manufacturing capacity is concentrated in a small number of countries, a fact that has become a concern for governments.
paragraphs.label: E

paragraphs.text: Batteries still wear out. Each cycle of charging and discharging causes small, irreversible changes to the electrodes, and a thin layer forms on the surface of the graphite that gradually consumes lithium. Heat speeds up these processes, as does keeping a battery fully charged for long periods, which is why many devices now stop charging at around eighty per cent unless the user overrides them. A typical phone battery loses a noticeable part of its capacity within a few years; the much larger batteries of electric cars, managed more carefully, often last considerably longer. Software in electric cars also keeps the battery within a narrow temperature range, heating or cooling it as needed.
paragraphs.label: F

paragraphs.text: The materials raise questions of their own. Many batteries use cobalt, much of which is mined in a single country under conditions that have been widely criticised, and nickel and lithium extraction can consume large amounts of water and energy. Manufacturers have responded by reducing the cobalt content of their electrodes, and some cheaper batteries now use an iron phosphate electrode that contains no cobalt or nickel at all, at the cost of storing somewhat less energy for the same weight. Some companies have begun to trace the origin of their materials more carefully in response to criticism.
paragraphs.label: G

paragraphs.text: Recycling is expected to become increasingly important as the first generation of electric cars reaches the end of its life. Recovering the valuable metals from used batteries is technically possible but has so far been expensive, and only a minority of lithium batteries are currently recycled. Researchers are also developing batteries that use sodium, which is far more abundant than lithium, or solid electrolytes, which could make batteries safer still. Whether any of these will replace lithium-ion technology remains uncertain, but its dominance is now being challenged for the first time in three decades. Batteries that are no longer suitable for cars can also be reused for less demanding purposes, such as storing electricity in buildings, before they are recycled.
paragraphs.label: H

paragraphs.text: The discovery that antibiotics could make farm animals grow faster was made almost by accident in the late 1940s, when researchers feeding animals the waste from antibiotic production noticed that they put on weight more quickly. Within a few years, small doses of antibiotics were being added routinely to animal feed in many countries. Today, in several parts of the world, more antibiotics are given to farm animals than to people. The practice has become one of the most contested questions in agriculture, because it is closely linked to the growing problem of bacteria that no longer respond to treatment. Few issues bring medicine and agriculture into such direct contact.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: The basic mechanism of resistance is not in dispute. Whenever antibiotics are used, bacteria that happen to survive them multiply, and the genes that allow them to survive can spread, sometimes passing between different species of bacteria. Clara Weiss, a microbiologist, points out that low doses given over long periods, as in growth promotion, create almost ideal conditions for resistance to develop, because they kill susceptible bacteria without eliminating those that are only partly resistant. In her view, using antibiotics to fatten animals is the least defensible use of these drugs anywhere. Resistance genes have been found in bacteria from soil and water far from any farm, showing how widely they can travel.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: How much farm use contributes to resistant infections in people is harder to establish. Resistant bacteria and resistance genes can travel from animals to humans through meat, through direct contact with animals and through water and soil contaminated by manure. Lars Holm, who studies public health, notes that such transfer has been documented clearly in some cases, but that most resistant infections in hospitals appear to arise from the use of antibiotics in human medicine. He argues that both sources matter and that arguing over which is more important has delayed action on both. Tracing a particular infection back to its source is difficult, because bacteria and genes can pass through many hosts along the way.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: Several countries banned the use of antibiotics as growth promoters decades ago, and their experience provides the best evidence of what such a ban achieves. In the first years, some farmers reported more disease among young animals, and the use of antibiotics for treatment rose for a time. After farmers improved hygiene, ventilation and vaccination, and gave young animals more time with their mothers, disease fell again and total antibiotic use ended well below its previous level. Samuel Otieno, a veterinarian who has advised on such changes, says that the lesson is that the drugs had been compensating for poor conditions. Some farmers also reduced the number of animals kept in each building.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: The economic effect of these bans has been smaller than opponents predicted. Priyanka Sen, an agricultural economist, reports that studies of countries that banned growth promoters found only small reductions in productivity, often less than one or two per cent, and that these were largely offset by lower spending on the drugs themselves. She cautions, however, that the results come mainly from wealthy countries with well-organised farms, and that the costs of improving conditions could be much harder to bear for small farmers in poorer regions, where demand for meat is growing fastest. Consumers in the countries concerned saw little change in the price of meat.
paragraphs.label: E

paragraphs.text: Enforcement is another difficulty. In some places antibiotics that are officially reserved for treating sick animals are still used routinely to prevent disease in whole herds, which can amount to growth promotion under another name. Otieno argues that the distinction between treatment and prevention is too easily blurred, and that the most effective rules are those that require a veterinarian to examine animals before any antibiotic is prescribed. Weiss adds that particular drugs regarded as critically important for human medicine should not be used in animals at all. Records of antibiotic sales are also incomplete in many countries, making it hard to know how much is used and for what purpose.
paragraphs.label: F

paragraphs.text: Consumers have also begun to influence practice. Large restaurant chains and supermarkets in several countries have announced that they will buy only meat raised without routine antibiotics, and some producers have changed their methods to meet these demands. Such commitments can move quickly, but they are difficult to verify and apply only to the markets where consumers are paying attention. Holm warns that voluntary commitments are no substitute for regulation, since they tend to shift problems to regions where scrutiny is weaker. Some commitments have been quietly weakened or postponed after the initial announcements.
paragraphs.label: G

paragraphs.text: The case against routine use of antibiotics in farming is strong, and the experience of countries that have restricted it suggests that animals can be raised efficiently without it. The more difficult question is how to extend these changes to places where farming is organised very differently and where the costs of change fall on people with the least ability to pay them. Because resistant bacteria cross borders easily, that question concerns everyone, not only the countries where the animals are raised. International agreements on the use of antibiotics in animals have been proposed but have so far made limited progress.
paragraphs.label: H
